title: Nodes That Never Loop
statement:
A directed graph has nodes `0` to `n - 1`. `graph[i]` is the list of nodes that node `i` points to. A node with an empty list is a **dead end**.

A node is **safe** if **every** path that starts at it ends in a dead end after a finite number of steps (so it cannot reach a cycle, and it is not on one). Return all safe nodes in **increasing order**.
constraints: 0 <= graph[i][j] < n; the total number of edges is at most 100000; a node may point to itself

examples.explanation: Nodes 0, 1 and 2 form a cycle, so none of them is safe. Node 3 is a dead end and node 4 leads only to it.
Every path ends at node 0, a dead end.

hints.nudge: Dead ends are safe. Which nodes become safe once you know that some nodes are safe?
hints.pattern: Peel the graph from the dead ends: reverse the edges, and repeatedly mark a node safe when all the nodes it points to are already safe (a topological sort on the reversed graph).
hints.pseudocode:
remaining[i] = number of nodes i points to; reverse[v] = the nodes that point to v
queue = all nodes with remaining 0 (dead ends)
while queue is not empty:
  v = pop; mark v safe
  for u in reverse[v]: remaining[u] -= 1; if remaining[u] == 0: push u
return the safe nodes in increasing order
hints.walkthrough: Following every path from every node to see whether it loops can take very long. Think in the other direction: a dead end is safe; a node is safe exactly when everything it points to is safe. So keep, for each node, how many of its targets are not known to be safe yet; start the queue with the nodes that have none (the dead ends). When a node is marked safe, every node pointing to it has one target fewer to wait for; if that count reaches 0, that node is safe as well. Nodes on a cycle (or leading into one) never reach 0, because a target on the cycle never becomes safe. A self-loop makes the count of that node never reach 0 as well. Finally list the safe nodes in increasing order. Each edge is looked at once: O(n + m).
